name: Times Square to Washington Square
blurb: Down Seventh Avenue through Times Square and Fifth past the Empire State, then back up Sixth to the park.

texts: Central Park opened in the late 1850s. Every lake and meadow in it was designed and built.
Central Park is larger than the whole country of Monaco.
Central Park has appeared in hundreds of films, more than almost any other place on Earth.
In the film Enchanted, from 2007, a whole musical number dances its way through Central Park, over Bow Bridge and past the boathouse.
The New York City Marathon finishes here in Central Park, every November.
The rocks in Central Park are Manhattan schist, scraped smooth by glaciers in the last ice age. You can still see the scratches.
Times Square was named in 1904, when The New York Times moved into the tower at its southern end.
A ball has dropped from the tower at One Times Square on New Year's Eve since the end of 1907.
City rules here require buildings to carry bright signs, so the lights of Times Square are part of the law.
Macy's at Herald Square fills an entire city block and was for many years called the largest store in the world.
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade ends here at Herald Square.
The Empire State Building went up in just over thirteen months, and opened in 1931.
The Empire State Building has its own zip code.
For nearly forty years, the Empire State Building was the tallest building in the world.
The Empire State Building is struck by lightning around twenty-five times a year. It was built to take it.
The Flatiron Building, from 1902, is only about two metres wide at its narrow end.
In the Spider-Man films, the Flatiron Building was home to the Daily Bugle, the newspaper Peter Parker works for.
Twice a year, in late May and mid July, the setting sun lines up exactly with Manhattan's cross streets. People call it Manhattanhenge.
Around the turn of the century, this neighbourhood was nicknamed Silicon Alley, for its wave of internet start-ups.
The marble arch in Washington Square was finished in the 1890s, to mark a century since Washington's inauguration.
Washington Square Park was once a potter's field, a public burial ground.
The two stone lions outside the New York Public Library are called Patience and Fortitude.
Bryant Park sits on top of the library's stacks: millions of books are kept underneath the lawn.
Radio City Music Hall opened in 1932, and its great stage curtain is said to be the largest in the world.
The Rockettes have danced at Radio City since the 1930s.
